# Self-Improvement {#sec-front-self-improvement}

A self-improving system changes itself: it generates its own training
signal, edits its own tools, or refines its own policy. This chapter
explains the design questions at the edge: where the improvement signal
comes from, why the loop can stall or diverge, and how to tell progress
from self-deception. By the end a reader can frame the self-improvement
problem and the trade-offs each approach makes.

## Problem

Human-labeled data and human feedback do not scale to every capability you
want. The system needs a signal it can generate and trust on its own,
without amplifying its own errors or gaming its own metric.

## Design

Closed improvement loops: self-generated data and curricula, model-graded
or verifier-based reward, and iterated distillation or fine-tuning on
filtered self-output. The open question is what makes such a loop converge
upward instead of collapsing.

## Evolution

From human-labeled fine-tuning, to reinforcement learning from human
feedback, to learning from AI feedback and self-play, to verifier-guided
self-training. Trace the move from human signal to self-generated signal
and why each step was attempted.

## Trade-offs

Self-generated signal scales and risks reward hacking, mode collapse, and
compounding bias. A stronger verifier buys reliability and pushes the
problem to whether the verifier is right. Each loop trades human oversight
for autonomy in the training process.

## In practice

Filtering and verification of self-output, detecting collapse and drift,
measuring real gain against a held-out and uncontaminated benchmark, and
the cost of an iterated loop.

## Foundations

The theory at the edge. Self-training and its fixed points, the conditions
for a self-improvement loop to converge rather than diverge, reward hacking
as objective misspecification, and what a verifier can and cannot certify.
